subject: ela
intro: Each problem gives you two informational texts about the same event or person. One is usually a firsthand account, written by someone who was there. The other is usually an outside account, written by an observer such as a biographer or reporter. Read both texts carefully, then answer the question. Your answer should be grounded in evidence from both passages, even when the texts are not worded the same way.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts of the same morning, then answer the question.

Memoir by Lena Okafor: "The harbor was still dark when I climbed into my little sailboat. My hands shook as I tied off the last rope, because I knew that if I made one mistake out there, no one would be close enough to help. I had practiced for two years, but practice is nothing like the real thing. When the wind finally caught my sail and pulled me out past the breakwater, I laughed and cried at the same time. I was the youngest person ever to attempt this crossing alone, and I could feel my whole future riding on the next four days."

Article by the Coastal Review: "On Tuesday at 5:40 a.m., Lena Okafor, 16, departed the Port Hadley marina in a 14-foot sailboat to begin a solo crossing of the strait. Okafor had trained for the attempt over two years with a local sailing club. If successful, she will become the youngest sailor to complete the route without a crew. Officials confirmed her departure and noted that weather conditions were calm at the time she left."

Both texts report the same basic fact about Lena's place in history. What is that shared fact, and how does each author present it differently?
items.answer: Both texts report that Lena is attempting to become the youngest person ever to make this solo crossing. The memoir presents this fact through Lena's own feelings, saying she could feel her whole future riding on the crossing, while the article presents the same fact plainly as a record she will set if she succeeds.

steps: Find a fact stated in both texts. The memoir says Lena was the youngest person ever to attempt the crossing alone; the article says she will become the youngest sailor to complete the route without a crew. This is the shared fact.
Look at how the memoir presents it: it is wrapped in emotion ('I could feel my whole future riding on the next four days'), giving the reader the inner experience.
Look at how the article presents it: it states the fact in a neutral, factual way ('she will become the youngest sailor to complete the route'), with a time, a place, and a boat size.
Combine these: the shared fact is Lena's record-setting youth, and the difference is that the memoir delivers it through feeling while the article delivers it as plain information.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts, then answer the question.

Firsthand account by Marcus Bell: "By the third hour of the storm, I had given up trying to keep the tent dry. Water ran in cold lines down the back of my neck, and the wind sounded like a freight train that never passed. I kept my flashlight on, not because I could see anything, but because the small circle of light made me feel less alone on the mountain. I told myself that if I could just hold on until morning, I would make it."

Report by the Mountain Rescue Bulletin: "At approximately 11 p.m., a sudden thunderstorm struck the eastern ridge, dropping nearly two inches of rain in three hours. One hiker, Marcus Bell, sheltered in place overnight at 9,200 feet. Rangers reached his position the following morning and confirmed he was unharmed. The bulletin reminds hikers to check forecasts, as conditions on the ridge can change within minutes."

How does each author's relationship to the events shape what their account is able to tell the reader?
items.answer: Marcus was inside the storm, so his firsthand account can tell the reader how the night felt, such as the cold water on his neck and the fear of being alone, details only the person there could know. The bulletin was written by outside observers, so it can tell the reader the measured facts, such as the time, the rainfall amount, and the altitude, along with a safety warning, but it cannot describe the inner experience.

steps: Identify each author's relationship to the events. Marcus is the firsthand participant who lived through the storm; the bulletin is written by an outside organization reporting afterward.
Connect Marcus's position to what he can tell: because he was there, he describes sensations and feelings (cold water, the train-like wind, feeling less alone) that only a participant would know.
Connect the bulletin's position to what it can tell: as an outside report, it gives measurable facts (time, rainfall, altitude) and a general safety reminder, but no inner feelings.
State the comparison: the firsthand position gives the felt experience, the outside position gives the verified facts and the broader lesson.

items.prompt:
Read both texts, then answer the question.

Memoir by inventor Priya Raman: "The first time my robot arm lifted the cup without crushing it, I sat down on the floor of my garage and stared at it for a long time. Six years. Six years of broken motors and burnt circuits and people telling me to find a normal job. I did not feel triumphant. Mostly I felt tired, and a little afraid that I had imagined the whole thing. I made it lift the cup four more times before I let myself believe it was real."

Profile by Tech Today: "Priya Raman, 34, spent six years developing a robotic arm capable of gripping fragile objects without damaging them. The breakthrough, achieved last spring in her home workshop, has since attracted interest from three medical-device companies. Raman credits persistence for her success, noting that early versions of the device failed repeatedly before she found a working design."

Name one detail the memoir includes about the moment of success that the profile leaves out, and explain why the memoir is able to include it.
items.answer: The memoir includes Priya's emotional reaction to the success, such as feeling tired and a little afraid rather than triumphant, and that she made the arm lift the cup several more times before she believed it was real. The profile leaves this out. The memoir can include it because Priya was the person living through the moment, so she knows her own private feelings, while the outside profile reports only what can be observed and confirmed.

steps: Scan the memoir for details about the success moment: she sat on the floor, felt tired and afraid rather than triumphant, and repeated the lift four more times before believing it.
Check the profile for those details: it reports the six years, the breakthrough timing, and company interest, but says nothing about her private feelings in that moment.
Choose a detail present only in the memoir (her emotional reaction or her disbelief) as the answer.
Explain the reason: as the firsthand participant, Priya can report her own inner experience, which an outside profile writer would have no way to observe.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts, then answer the question.

Firsthand account by firefighter Dana Cole: "We rolled up to the warehouse and I could feel the heat through the truck door before I even opened it. My job was the back entrance. I remember counting my breaths to stay calm, the way we are trained, while smoke poured out around the frame. When we finally got the last worker out and into the air, somebody started clapping, but I did not hear it until much later. In the moment, all I could hear was my own heartbeat."

News article by the City Ledger: "A fire broke out Saturday evening at a warehouse on Fulton Street. Firefighters from Station 12 responded within six minutes and evacuated all eleven employees without injury. The cause is under investigation. The fire chief praised the crew's coordination, calling the rescue a model of training and teamwork."

Both texts describe the rescue of the workers. State one way the two accounts emphasize different things, using evidence from each.
items.answer: The firsthand account emphasizes the personal, sensory experience of the rescue, such as feeling the heat through the truck door and hearing only her own heartbeat, while the news article emphasizes the measurable outcome and the bigger picture, such as the six-minute response time, the eleven employees evacuated without injury, and the chief's praise for teamwork. Each focuses on a different layer of the same event.

steps: Confirm the shared event: both texts describe firefighters rescuing the warehouse workers.
Pull evidence of the firsthand emphasis: Dana focuses on her own senses and feelings (heat through the door, counting breaths, hearing only her heartbeat).
Pull evidence of the article's emphasis: it focuses on facts and results (response time, eleven employees, no injuries, the chief's praise).
State the contrast clearly, naming the personal/sensory emphasis of one and the factual/outcome emphasis of the other.

items.prompt:
Read both texts, then answer the question.

Memoir by athlete Sofia Reyes: "When the gun went off, I forgot everything my coaches had told me. I forgot my pace plan, I forgot the cameras, I forgot the eighty thousand people in the stands. There was only the track and the runner just ahead of me. With twenty meters left, my legs felt like they belonged to someone else, but something inside me refused to slow down. I crossed the line and did not even know I had won until I saw my own name flash on the board."

Biography excerpt: "Sofia Reyes won the 400-meter final by a margin of four hundredths of a second, setting a national record of 49.18. Analysts noted that her closing speed in the final twenty meters was the fastest in the field. Reyes had finished fourth at the previous championship, making the victory a significant turnaround in her career."

How does the difference between the authors' points of view lead them to describe the final twenty meters of the race differently?
items.answer: Because Sofia is writing from inside her own experience, she describes the final twenty meters through feeling, saying her legs felt like they belonged to someone else but something refused to slow down. Because the biographer is an outside observer, the same twenty meters are described through measured analysis, noting that her closing speed was the fastest in the field. The firsthand point of view gives the inner sensation, and the outside point of view gives the recorded performance.

steps: Locate the shared moment both texts describe: the final twenty meters of the race.
Note Sofia's point of view as a participant and how it shapes her description: she reports the physical sensation and inner drive she felt.
Note the biographer's outside point of view and how it shapes the description: the same stretch becomes a data point, the fastest closing speed in the field.
Connect point of view to presentation: the insider tells how it felt, the outside observer tells what the numbers showed.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts, then answer the question.

Firsthand account by relief worker Tomas Vega: "We landed two days after the earthquake, and the first thing I noticed was how quiet everything was. No traffic, no music, just people moving slowly through the dust. A grandmother handed me a cup of tea she had made over a small fire, even though she had lost her home. I have worked in many hard places, but I have never been so humbled by someone's kindness in the middle of their own loss."

Report by the Global Aid Council: "A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck the region on March 4, damaging an estimated 12,000 buildings and displacing roughly 40,000 residents. Relief teams arrived within 48 hours and established three supply centers. The council reports that food and clean water reached affected areas faster than in previous disasters of similar scale."

What does a reader understand about the earthquake from reading both texts together that neither text gives alone?
items.answer: Reading both together, a reader understands both the human, personal side of the disaster and its measurable scale. From Tomas the reader learns how the survivors lived through it, including the quiet, the dust, and a grandmother's kindness amid her own loss. From the report the reader learns the magnitude, the 12,000 damaged buildings, the 40,000 displaced residents, and the speed of relief. Together they give a fuller picture, the felt human experience and the large-scale facts, that neither account provides on its own.

steps: Identify what only the firsthand account gives: the personal, human moments, such as the quiet, the dust, and the grandmother's kindness.
Identify what only the report gives: the scale and facts, such as magnitude, buildings damaged, residents displaced, and relief speed.
Explain why each alone is incomplete: the memoir lacks the scale, the report lacks the human feeling.
State the combined insight: together they show both the human experience and the large-scale facts, a fuller picture than either alone.

items.prompt:
Read both texts, then answer the question.

Memoir by astronaut Helen Park: "The moment we lost gravity, my pencil drifted up off the console and just hung there in the air. I had read about weightlessness in a hundred manuals, but reading is not the same as watching your own pencil float past your face. My stomach lurched, then settled. I spent the first ten minutes simply pushing off the walls like a child, grinning, before I remembered I had a checklist to complete."

Encyclopedia entry: "During spaceflight, astronauts experience microgravity, a condition in which objects and people appear to float because they are in continuous free fall around Earth. Newly arrived crew members commonly report temporary disorientation and nausea, known as space adaptation syndrome, which usually resolves within a few days as the body adjusts."

Both texts describe the experience of weightlessness. Explain how each author's purpose shapes the way they present it.
items.answer: Helen's purpose is to share her personal experience, so she presents weightlessness through a specific, vivid moment, the pencil floating past her face and pushing off the walls like a child. The encyclopedia's purpose is to explain the science clearly to any reader, so it presents weightlessness through a general definition of microgravity and the common reaction astronauts have. One author makes the reader feel the moment, the other makes the reader understand the concept.

steps: Determine each author's purpose: the memoir aims to share a personal experience; the encyclopedia aims to explain a concept generally.
Show how the memoir's purpose shapes it: it uses one vivid, specific scene (the floating pencil, pushing off walls).
Show how the encyclopedia's purpose shapes it: it gives a general definition and the typical reaction, applicable to all astronauts.
State the comparison: the purposes differ, so one presentation makes the reader feel the moment and the other helps the reader understand the science.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts, then answer the question.

Firsthand account by teacher Amara Diallo: "The day the new library opened, I watched a boy named Eli walk in, stop, and just look up at the shelves with his mouth open. He had told me weeks before that he did not like reading. That afternoon he checked out three books and asked if he could come back the next day. I have taught for fifteen years, and that single moment reminded me why I started."

Newspaper article: "The Lincoln Community Library opened its doors on Monday after a two-year fundraising campaign raised $480,000. The 8,000-square-foot facility houses more than 20,000 volumes and offers free internet access. Organizers expect the library to serve roughly 6,000 residents in the surrounding neighborhood."

Name one way the two accounts differ in the kind of detail they include, and connect that difference to each author's relationship to the event.
items.answer: The firsthand account includes a small personal detail, the story of one boy named Eli discovering books, because Amara was present and personally connected to her students. The newspaper article includes large-scale facts, such as the $480,000 raised, the 8,000 square feet, and the 20,000 volumes, because the reporter is an outside observer summarizing the project for the public. One author tells a single human story she witnessed, the other reports the overall numbers an outsider would gather.

steps: Compare the kinds of detail: the memoir gives one personal story (Eli), the article gives numbers (money raised, square footage, volumes, residents served).
Tie the memoir's details to Amara's relationship: she is an insider, a teacher present at the opening, so she notices and cares about one student's moment.
Tie the article's details to the reporter's relationship: an outside observer reports the broad facts useful to the general public.
State the difference plainly, naming the personal-story detail of one and the large-scale facts of the other, each linked to the author's position.

items.prompt:
Read both texts, then answer the question.

Memoir by sailor Captain Ruiz: "We had been becalmed for six days when the wind finally returned. I will not pretend I was calm. Our water was nearly gone, and I had begun to wonder if I had made a terrible mistake bringing the crew out so far. When the sails snapped full again, one of the younger sailors began to sing, and the rest of us joined in, voices cracking. I have never been so grateful for a simple breeze."

Biography excerpt: "Captain Ruiz's 1889 voyage encountered an unusually long calm in the central ocean, stalling the vessel for nearly a week. Historians note that the crew's water supply ran dangerously low during this period. When favorable winds returned, the ship completed the remaining distance in nine days, arriving only slightly behind schedule."

Both texts report that the ship was stalled by a long calm. How does the memoir add to what the biography reports about this period?
items.answer: The biography reports the calm as a factual event, noting it lasted nearly a week, that the water supply ran dangerously low, and that the ship still arrived only slightly behind schedule. The memoir adds the human experience of that same period, such as Captain Ruiz's fear that he had made a terrible mistake, the crew's gratitude when the wind returned, and the moment they all sang together with cracking voices. The memoir adds the emotions and personal meaning that the factual biography leaves out.

steps: Identify the shared event: a long calm stalled the ship and the water ran low.
List what the biography provides: duration, low water supply, and the on-time-ish arrival, all as outside facts.
List what the memoir adds: the captain's fear and self-doubt and the crew singing in gratitude when the wind returned.
State that the memoir adds the inner, emotional experience of the period, which the outside biography does not capture.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts, then answer the question.

Firsthand account by scientist Dr. Lin Wei: "I had checked the readings four times, and they still made no sense. The samples from the deep vent contained a microbe that, as far as I knew, should not be able to survive without sunlight. My hands were actually trembling as I prepared the slide. When I looked through the microscope and saw it moving, alive, I had to step away and breathe before I trusted my own eyes."

Science journal summary: "In a 2014 study, researchers identified a previously unknown microorganism living near a deep-sea hydrothermal vent. The organism derives energy through chemosynthesis rather than photosynthesis, allowing it to thrive in the absence of sunlight. The discovery expanded scientific understanding of the conditions under which life can exist."

Explain how the firsthand account and the outside summary present the same discovery for different reasons.
items.answer: Dr. Lin Wei presents the discovery as a personal, suspenseful moment because her purpose is to share the experience of making it, describing her trembling hands and her need to step away and breathe. The journal summary presents the same discovery as established knowledge because its purpose is to inform the scientific community, explaining that the microbe survives through chemosynthesis and what the finding means for understanding life. The firsthand account focuses on the experience of discovery, the summary focuses on the result and its significance.

steps: Identify the shared discovery: a microbe living without sunlight near a deep-sea vent.
Note the firsthand author's purpose, to convey the lived experience, shown by her trembling hands and disbelief.
Note the summary's purpose, to inform readers of the result, shown by its calm explanation of chemosynthesis and significance.
Connect purpose to presentation: differing purposes lead one to dramatize the moment and the other to state the finding plainly.

items.prompt:
Read both texts, then answer the question.

Memoir by musician Carlos Mendez: "The night of my first big concert, I broke a guitar string halfway through the opening song. For one horrible second, I thought it was all over. Then I remembered something my grandfather told me: the audience does not want perfection, they want you. So I kept playing on five strings and smiled like nothing had happened. By the end, I think it was the best show of my life, broken string and all."

Review by Music Weekly: "Carlos Mendez delivered a confident debut performance on Friday to a sold-out crowd. Despite a minor equipment issue early in the set, the young guitarist maintained his composure and earned a standing ovation. Critics praised his stage presence and his ability to connect with the audience."

Both texts mention the broken string. State the difference in how each account treats it, and explain what causes that difference.
items.answer: The memoir treats the broken string as a major personal turning point, describing the horrible second when Carlos thought it was over and the advice from his grandfather that helped him recover. The review treats it as a minor equipment issue mentioned in passing while praising his composure. The difference comes from each author's relationship to the event: Carlos lived the inner panic and recovery, so it felt large to him, while the outside reviewer saw only a smooth performance and so reports it as a small detail.

steps: Find the shared detail: a string broke during the performance.
Describe the memoir's treatment: a dramatic personal turning point with fear, memory of advice, and recovery.
Describe the review's treatment: a passing mention of a minor equipment issue, focused on his composure.
Explain the cause: the insider felt the inner panic so it looms large; the outside reviewer only saw the polished result, so it is minor to him.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts, then answer the question.

Firsthand account by pilot Grace Tan: "When the engine warning light came on, I did exactly what my training told me to do, but my mind was racing the whole time. I radioed the tower, I scanned for a place to land, and I kept my voice steady so the passengers would not panic. Inside, though, I was terrified. We touched down safely on a quiet airstrip, and only then did I let myself feel my own hands shaking on the controls."

Aviation report: "On June 12, a small aircraft piloted by Grace Tan reported an engine warning and performed a precautionary landing at a regional airstrip. All four passengers were unharmed. Investigators later traced the warning to a faulty sensor rather than an actual engine failure. The pilot was commended for following emergency procedures correctly."

What can the firsthand account tell the reader that the official report cannot, and why?
items.answer: The firsthand account can tell the reader how the emergency felt to the pilot, such as her racing mind, her terror, and her hands shaking only after landing, while she kept her voice steady for the passengers. The official report cannot tell this because it is written by outside investigators who can confirm only observable facts, such as the warning, the safe landing, and the faulty sensor. Only Grace, who lived the event, knows her own private fear and effort to stay calm.

steps: Identify what is unique to the firsthand account: Grace's inner state, her racing mind, terror, and shaking hands hidden behind a steady voice.
Identify what the report covers: observable, verifiable facts, the warning, safe landing, unharmed passengers, faulty sensor.
Explain why the report cannot give the inner state: outside investigators can only document what is observable, not private feelings.
State the answer: the firsthand account gives the hidden inner experience because only the participant has access to it.

items.prompt:
Read both texts, then answer the question.

Memoir by activist Naomi Cohen: "We had marched for three hours, and my feet ached, but I barely noticed. All around me, strangers were chanting the same words I had whispered alone in my room for years. A woman I had never met linked her arm through mine. For the first time in my life, I did not feel like I was fighting by myself. That feeling, more than any speech, is what I will remember."

History textbook excerpt: "The march drew an estimated 15,000 participants and lasted roughly four hours, ending at the city hall steps. Organizers presented a petition to local officials. The event is now regarded by historians as a turning point that increased public support for the reform, which passed the following year."

Explain how reading both accounts gives a fuller understanding of the march than reading either one alone.
items.answer: The textbook gives the outside facts and the long-term significance of the march, such as the 15,000 participants, the four-hour length, the petition, and the reform that passed the next year. The memoir gives the inner human experience of being there, such as the feeling of no longer fighting alone and a stranger linking arms with Naomi. Reading both together lets the reader understand both why the march mattered historically and how it actually felt to take part, which neither account provides by itself.

steps: Identify what the textbook supplies: size, duration, the petition, and the historical outcome.
Identify what the memoir supplies: the personal feeling of solidarity and a specific human moment.
Note each one's limit: the textbook lacks the human feeling, the memoir lacks the scale and outcome.
Combine them into one insight: together they show both the historical importance and the lived experience of the march.

items.prompt:
Read both accounts, then answer the question.

Firsthand account by chef Iris Bennett: "For the final round, I drew an ingredient I had never cooked with in my life: sea urchin. I had ninety seconds to decide what to do, and I could feel the judges watching. My grandmother's voice came into my head, telling me to cook what I knew, so I built the dish around flavors from her kitchen instead of trying to impress anyone. When the head judge took a bite and closed his eyes, I knew I had made the right choice."

Magazine profile: "Iris Bennett won the national cooking championship after a final round featuring a rare ingredient, sea urchin. Judges praised her dish for its bold yet familiar flavors. Bennett, who learned to cook from her grandmother, has since opened her own restaurant and published a cookbook drawing on family recipes."

Both texts mention the influence of Iris's grandmother. How does each account present that influence differently?
items.answer: The memoir presents the grandmother's influence as a real-time, internal moment during the competition, with her voice coming into Iris's head and telling her to cook what she knew. The profile presents the same influence as a general background fact, noting that Iris learned to cook from her grandmother and now draws on family recipes. The firsthand account shows the influence shaping a specific decision in the moment, while the outside profile reports it as a broad biographical detail.

steps: Find the shared element: the grandmother's influence on Iris.
Describe the memoir's presentation: an in-the-moment internal voice guiding a specific decision during the final round.
Describe the profile's presentation: a general fact of her background and how it shapes her cooking overall.
State the contrast: one shows the influence acting in a single moment, the other states it as a broad biographical fact.

items.prompt:
Read both texts, then answer the question.

Memoir by explorer Ana Sorbo: "By the time we reached the cave's deepest chamber, our lamps were dim and my heart was pounding from more than the climb. When my light touched the wall, I stopped breathing. There were paintings there, handprints and animals, made by people thousands of years ago. I reached out but did not touch them. It felt like standing in someone's memory. None of us spoke for a long time."

Archaeology bulletin: "A team led by Ana Sorbo documented previously unrecorded cave paintings in a remote chamber. The images, including handprints and animal figures, are estimated to be over 9,000 years old. The team photographed the site without disturbing it, and the findings have been submitted for further study by specialists."

Both texts report that the paintings were left undisturbed. Explain why each author emphasizes this fact in a different way.
items.answer: The memoir emphasizes leaving the paintings undisturbed as a deeply personal, reverent choice, with Ana reaching out but not touching and feeling like she stood in someone's memory while no one spoke. The bulletin emphasizes the same fact as proper scientific procedure, stating that the team photographed the site without disturbing it for further study. The firsthand account presents it as an emotional act of respect, while the outside bulletin presents it as following correct method.

steps: Identify the shared fact: the paintings were left undisturbed.
Describe the memoir's emphasis: a reverent, emotional choice, reaching out but not touching, feeling like standing in someone's memory.
Describe the bulletin's emphasis: a matter of scientific procedure, photographing without disturbing the site for study.
Explain the difference: the participant frames it as personal respect, the outside report frames it as correct method, reflecting their different purposes and points of view.
